name: The Hound's Swallet
resident: the down wolves of Hound Down, the pelters who follow them down for their skins, and at the bottom, by the water, the Old Hound
story: A lost bourne went into the chalk here and hollowed the down on its way to the Mere: round bores, a lake, a shaft of daylight where the roof fell in. The Vale says the Chalk Hound was cut on the hill above to keep one hound asleep, and that it sleeps down here. A scourer's white cord runs down the wall from the throat to the deepest chamber, taut all the way.
unique_object: Aldous Hounder's white scouring cord, tied on at the lodge gate a mile away, running down the swallet's walls to a rake-head in the Old Hound's den

rooms.note: where the roof fell in: the pelters' drying-frames under the shaft of light
the lost bourne's water, still and clear, going nowhere
the bourne's old bore, lit by what grows on the chalk where the water stood
where the pack lies up: bones, fur, and the rake-heads of scourers who came down after them

name: Knappers' Deep
resident: the Larkbourne Boys in the upper galleries, digging floorstone to sell; past the Fall, the night shift the roof came down on, and their overman
story: Galleries cut along the floorstone seam through the white chalk, propped with oak where the chalk is rotten, lit by the miners' lanterns where anybody still works. The Boys have the near face and a camp in the first gallery. They go no further than the Fall at night. Past it the galleries are as the night shift left them, except that the night shift is still in them.
unique_object: the overman's tally-stick, notched for the eight of them, in the hand of the thing at the far face that is still counting

rooms.note: the foot of the shaft: the ladder going up into a square of daylight
the Boys' camp in the first gallery: their fire, their sacks of floorstone, their bedrolls
the near face of the floorstone, the seam showing black in the white, where the Boys dig
the Fall: where the roof came down eleven winters ago, a hill of chalk under a hole of daylight
where the seam broke off over an older working nobody knew was there
the night shift's gallery, their picks in the face where they left them

features.name: an old prospect of the Deep

name: The Throat under the Hum Stone
resident: the barrow-diggers in the upper vaults; past them the Hush's dead, come down after the hum; at the bottom, the diggers' king and the thing he is ringing
story: Under the stone the Builders cut a throat into the chalk and faced it with their fused stone: vaults that step down and down toward the Hush, built, the Sayers would say, to hold a note. The diggers broke in at the top and have been carrying out bronze ever since. The deeper vaults are where the hum comes from, and the dead have found their way into them.
unique_object: the throat's bronze plate, a bell with no curve to it, which the diggers' king has been ringing to keep the dead standing still

rooms.note: where the diggers broke through the Builders' door: shoring, spoil, their lanterns
the diggers' camp in the first vault, their bronze in sacks
where the stone's root comes down through the vault, and the diggers' first hole lets the daylight in
rows of niches: whoever kept the note lies here, in no order the Vale would understand
a rift across the vault where the hum comes up loudest
the Hush's dead stand here in rows, facing down the throat, listening

features.name: a rubbing taken off a niche

name: The Crypt under Wake Barrow
formed_by: the first people of the downs, then the barrow-wives
resident: the Ash Winter's dead, the wakeless, laid down unwatched; down wolves come in by an oak's root after the bones; at the bottom, Ebba Crowle, the last barrow-wife, still sitting her wake
story: The barrow's passage goes in under the façade and down, a stair at a time, into rooms the first people cut in the chalk and the barrow-wives kept: the side cists of the first dead, the wake hall where the dead were laid on benches to be sat with, the pool where they were washed, and the niches where the Ash Winter's dead were put, more of them than the Vale has ever said it lost. Ebba Crowle went down past all of them with her lamp, to the last hall, and sat down.
unique_object: Ebba Crowle's lamp, a horn lantern with a wick of plaited rush, that burned at the bottom of the barrow for two hundred years and has gone out

rooms.note: the stone passage behind the façade, the Crowles' candles stuck on every ledge and burnt down
the side cists, where the downs' first dead lie under their slabs, two of the slabs pushed off from inside
where the wakes were sat: benches cut in the chalk round the walls, the dead laid on them, the barrow-wives' stools between
a chalk spring in a basin where the barrow-wives washed the dead before the wake
where an oak's root broke the roof: the daylight comes down it from the Wake Oaks, and the down wolves come down it after the bones
the Ash Winter's dead in rows of niches, each with a rush-light burnt out at its head

name: The Cellars under Wassail Knap
formed_by: the press-masters of the Great Press, cut down into the chalk under the knap a vault at a time
resident: the last Wassail King's wassailers and the pickers who followed the singing down, still at the revel; the orchard's dead pickers, buried under their trees, come down through the roots; at the bottom, Hob Applegarth, the Wassail King, at the Mother Vat
story: A stair from the cellar-head down into the vaults the press-masters cut for the Great Press's cider: the pomace cellar where the cheeses of crushed apple were stacked to drain, the long barrel run, the wassail hall where the Vale feasted the King on Twelfth Night, the vat hall, the press-spring where the water was drawn, the King's table, and at the bottom the Mother Vat, the oldest cask in the Vale, that the wassail woke every year. The press-master barred the stair at dawn on a King who would not give back his crown, and the revel has gone round the vats for forty years.
unique_object: the Wassail Crown, plaited of the Mother Pippin's withies, still green

rooms.note: the foot of the cellar stair, the press-master's bar still on the inside of the door
racks of crushed-apple cheeses gone to black, forty years draining
the King's feast laid on the long tables, the fire never let out, the wassailers asleep where they fell dancing
the great vats in rows, hooped in black iron, singing when the wind is in the grates
the spring the press drew its water from, and the pickers' bones under the roots that have come down to drink
the high table, the King's chair empty, a place laid for everybody who ever went down

name: The Undercroft of the Great Barn
formed_by: the tithe-reeves of Southgate, who vaulted granaries under the barn in the dressed chalk and let daylight down to the grain through louvres
resident: bristlebacks fat on the rotten tithe, the sheaf-men wound out of it, the reapers who brought the last harvest in, laid in the straw and not got up, and the Kern Mother in the sheaf hall
story: A stair down from the threshing floor into the tithe-reeves' undercroft: the granary under the fallen floor with the sky coming in, the drying kiln and its flue, the reapers' loft where the last harvest's gang lay down in the straw, the tithe vault, and the sheaf hall where the kern-baby was hung from the tie-beam over winter fifty years ago and never carried out.
unique_object: the kern-knot, the plaited heart of the last sheaf, with a whole harvest's life still in it

rooms.note: the foot of the barn stair, chaff ankle-deep
the granary under the threshing floor, the floor fallen in on the grain and the sky coming down through it
where the last harvest's gang lay down in the straw to sleep off the harvest supper and did not get up
